section_summary: This section concerns protection of American copyrights in Japan, especially unauthorized translations, pirated editions, and a 1936 Tokyo court decision involving Dr. Wilhelm Plage. Embassy reports and correspondence examine the 1905 United States–Japan copyright convention, Japan’s Berne Convention reservations, and the possible effects of United States adherence. Later documents identify Japanese translations of American books, including Gone with the Wind, and circulate the Embassy’s findings to officials, publishers, and authors.

subfiles.title: File note on W. Jefferson Davis book piracy
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum on a pirated Japanese edition of Davis’s book and copyright treaty policy.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references the Davis piracy case and Policy Memorandum 652.

subfiles.title: File note on copyright protection in China and Japan
subfiles.about: Cross-references a conversation with publisher Charles E. Keck.
subfiles.summary: Notes Keck’s discussion of copyright protection in China and Japan.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese copyright laws
subfiles.about: Points to a report enclosing Japanese copyright laws and regulations.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references a report and copies of Japanese laws and regulations.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about unauthorized publication in Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether later treaties or protocols affect Japanese publication of copyrighted American works.
subfiles.summary: Counsel for publishers requests current treaty information after finding an older Copyright Office bulletin.

subfiles.title: Reply on United States–Japan copyright agreements
subfiles.from: Green H. Hackworth, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Supplies the 1905 copyright convention and 1908 China trade-mark convention.
subfiles.summary: States that no later United States–Japan copyright agreement exists and suggests contacting the Department of Commerce for Japanese copyright law.

subfiles.title: Instruction concerning a Tokyo copyright ruling
subfiles.about: Requests the Japanese court decision reported in Variety and information on infringements of American copyrights.
subfiles.summary: Directs the Embassy to obtain and translate the ruling and report known infringement cases.

subfiles.title: Court ruling favors copyright piracy, already common, in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports reversal of a copyright ruling in a case brought by Wilhelm Plage.
subfiles.summary: The article says Judge Fujishima held that only the injured copyright owner could bring the action. It describes allegedly unauthorized productions of Alt Heidelberg and Madam Butterfly and warns of difficulty enforcing foreign rights.

subfiles.title: File note on Rome revision of the Berne Convention
subfiles.about: Cross-references an inquiry into Japanese enforcement of copyright without formalities.
subfiles.summary: Points to an instruction concerning the 1928 Rome revision and Japanese court practice.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on Japanese copyright judgment
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Embassy’s report on American copyright protection in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Notes reliance on Japanese copyright law and the Embassy’s lack of known current infringement cases.

subfiles.title: International copyright judgment
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Investigates the December 1936 Tokyo Local Court decision involving Wilhelm Plage and foreign theatrical copyrights.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reconstructs Plage’s complaint over performances of Alt Heidelberg and Madam Butterfly and explains that the criminal case failed because assignments had not been registered before infringement. It regards the lower-court ruling as narrow and doubts that it sets a broad precedent against foreign copyrights. The despatch reviews American protection under Japanese law and argues that United States adherence to the Berne Convention would improve protection.

subfiles.title: Confidential letter to Senator Duffy
subfiles.about: Relays Embassy findings relevant to Senate consideration of the Berne Convention.
subfiles.summary: McClure follows up on John G. Paine’s testimony about a Japanese copyright case. He quotes the Embassy’s account of limited current protection and its view that Berne adherence would help American authors.

subfiles.title: Confidential letter to Senator Pittman
subfiles.about: Provides Embassy findings on Japanese copyright protection during Senate treaty consideration.
subfiles.summary: McClure quotes the Embassy’s view that American works face inadequate protection and that adherence to the Berne Convention could improve enforcement in Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Embassy despatch to Commerce
subfiles.about: Sends the Embassy’s copyright judgment report for interested commercial organizations.
subfiles.summary: McClure suggests sharing the despatch’s substance with copyright interests without attributing outside communications to the Department or Embassy.

subfiles.title: Letter to the Register of Copyrights
subfiles.about: Forwards the Embassy’s investigation of the ruling first reported in Variety.
subfiles.summary: McClure recounts the inquiry prompted by Bouvé and Paine’s testimony and encloses despatch No. 2486.

subfiles.title: Commerce acknowledgment of Embassy despatch
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Japanese court despatch and plans to circulate its findings.
subfiles.summary: Brown will share the ruling with relevant Commerce divisions and preserve the requested limits on attribution.

subfiles.title: Commerce letter quoting Kilroe’s criticism
subfiles.about: Relays Edwin P. Kilroe’s disagreement with the Embassy’s view of possible Berne protection.
subfiles.summary: Kilroe argues that Japan retained formalities and translation rights, cites the 1905 bilateral convention, and contends Berne adherence would not protect American translations. He reports widespread piracy, including Shirley Temple song albums.

subfiles.title: Kilroe letter enclosing copyright materials
subfiles.about: Sends a compilation concerning the Plage case and copyright protection in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Kilroe encloses commentary, legal opinion, clippings, and Doyle’s letter, and promises information from solicitors in England and Japan.

subfiles.title: Copyright protection of works of foreign authors in Japan: contents and case statement
subfiles.about: Introduces the Plage case and lists materials in Kilroe’s enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes the ruling and lists critiques, clippings, and a Japanese legal opinion.

subfiles.title: Discussion and criticism by N. D. Golden
subfiles.about: Analyzes the Tokyo court decision and its implications for foreign copyright owners.
subfiles.summary: Golden explains that the failed criminal complaint involved unregistered assignments, not a general rejection of foreign copyright. He treats the ruling as limited and argues that United States adherence to the Berne Convention would strengthen American rights in Japan.

subfiles.title: Criticism by Edwin P. Kilroe
subfiles.about: Disputes Golden’s interpretation of Japanese reservations and the 1905 treaty.
subfiles.summary: Kilroe argues that Berne adherence alone would not protect American works against unauthorized Japanese translations. He cites Japan’s reservations and the bilateral treaty and reports piracy of American music.

subfiles.title: Copyright battle renewed by Plage
subfiles.about: Reports seizure of thousands of music volumes in Plage’s continuing copyright litigation.
subfiles.summary: Plage obtains attachment of Shunjusha publications and plans a civil action against Shochiku.

subfiles.title: European agent’s copyright suits
subfiles.about: Fragmentary clipping concerning copyright suits threatened by a European agent.
subfiles.summary: Only portions of the headline and text remain legible.

subfiles.title: Plage contradicts compromise rumor
subfiles.about: Describes Plage’s royalty demands and planned music copyright actions.
subfiles.summary: Two copies of the same clipping report that Plage rejects rumors of reduced settlements, seeks royalties from performances and films, and organizes collection arrangements for musicians.

subfiles.title: Opinion on the Plage judgment
subfiles.about: Explains why the Tokyo court rejected Plage’s copyright complaint.
subfiles.summary: The lawyers state that the Berne treaty did not govern assignments, so Japanese registration requirements applied. They conclude that the unregistered assignees lacked standing under copyright law, while a civil damages claim might remain possible.

subfiles.title: Doyle letter about Plage’s prospects
subfiles.about: Assesses Plage’s litigation and the business risk of association with it.
subfiles.summary: Doyle doubts Plage will succeed in Japanese courts and worries that involvement would harm Fox’s Shochiku relationship.

subfiles.title: Native Production
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese film producers’ objections to postponed Berne revision and industry expansion.
subfiles.summary: Producers seek clarification of music and scenario rights; the clipping also covers new Japanese film ventures.

subfiles.title: Letter to McGraw enclosing Embassy copyright study
subfiles.about: Forwards the Embassy’s December 1938 study of American copyrights in Japan.
subfiles.summary: McClure says the study may interest McGraw despite adding little to his original inquiry.

subfiles.title: Variety article on piracy of foreign songs
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese publication and recording of foreign music without permission.
subfiles.summary: Crane describes cheap sheet-music copying and weak prospects for effective damage suits.

subfiles.title: Follow-up letter to Kilroe
subfiles.about: Asks whether Kilroe has received promised information from solicitors abroad.
subfiles.summary: McClure offers to consider further Embassy investigation if Kilroe remains interested.

subfiles.title: Kilroe reply on further copyright information
subfiles.about: Promises information from English and Japanese solicitors and welcomes Embassy research.
subfiles.summary: Kilroe has received the material but has not yet reviewed it.

subfiles.title: American copyrights in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Studies copyright protection, translation rights, and Japanese publication of American works.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reads the 1905 bilateral convention as protecting American originals without Japanese registration while expressly allowing unauthorized translations. It explains Japan’s ten-year Berne translation reservation and warns that Berne adherence might not help Americans unless the bilateral convention changes. A partial list identifies many apparent Japanese translations, including Gone with the Wind. The Embassy considers limited royalties more negotiable than a foreign owner’s right to block translation.

subfiles.title: Letter to Taft about Gone with the Wind
subfiles.about: Forwards the Embassy study and highlights its list of apparent Japanese translations.
subfiles.summary: Alerts Taft to the listing of Gone with the Wind and sends copies to other interested parties.

subfiles.title: Second copy of letter to McGraw
subfiles.about: Forwards the Embassy’s December 1938 copyright study.
subfiles.summary: A separate filed copy of the letter appearing on page 50.

subfiles.title: Letter to Mrs. Marsh about Japanese translations
subfiles.about: Reports apparent unauthorized Japanese translations of Gone with the Wind.
subfiles.summary: McClure encloses the Taft letter, notes related notifications, and discusses continuing attention to the pending copyright treaty.

subfiles.title: Letter to George P. Brett Jr.
subfiles.about: Sends materials about a Japanese translation of Gone with the Wind.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the Taft letter and accompanying Embassy despatch.

subfiles.title: Letter to Stevens Mitchell
subfiles.about: Sends materials about a Japanese translation of Gone with the Wind.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the Taft letter and accompanying Embassy despatch.

subfiles.title: Letter requesting Commerce comment
subfiles.about: Forwards Embassy despatch No. 3512 for Commerce Department review.
subfiles.summary: McClure requests comment on the despatch’s notable findings.

subfiles.title: Letter requesting Deák’s comment
subfiles.about: Seeks comment on Japan’s expected position at Berne revision talks.
subfiles.summary: McClure reports that Japanese representatives may seek to remove translation protection and might accept low royalties while rejecting a foreign owner’s right to prohibit translation.

subfiles.title: Letter requesting Copyright Office comment
subfiles.about: Sends Embassy despatch No. 3512 to the Register of Copyrights.
subfiles.summary: McClure requests the Copyright Office’s comment on the despatch.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Embassy copyright despatch
subfiles.about: Commends the Embassy’s American copyrights study and requests further information.
subfiles.summary: The Department praises despatch No. 3512 and welcomes similar reporting.

subfiles.title: The copyright situation in Japan
subfiles.about: Assesses despatch No. 3512 and plans its circulation and policy follow-up.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum interprets the Embassy’s account of protection for originals and the 1905 convention’s translation exception. It suggests terminating the bilateral convention if the United States joins Berne, notes possible Japanese interest in compulsory licensing, and proposes notifying publishers, authors, agencies, and Professor Deák.

subfiles.title: Instruction enclosing Margaret Mitchell letter
subfiles.about: Sends Mitchell’s October 1939 letter concerning Gone with the Wind.
subfiles.summary: Draws Embassy attention to the letter’s second paragraph.

subfiles.title: Copyright Office reply on Japanese translation rights
subfiles.about: Comments on the Embassy’s report about unauthorized translations under the 1905 treaty and Berne Convention.
subfiles.summary: The letter confirms that the 1905 treaty permits unauthorized translations and discusses Japan’s ten-year Berne reservation. It considers whether that treaty would continue to deny American authors translation rights after United States adherence to Berne, and notes Japan’s possible demand for broader freedom to translate. The letter continues beyond this section.
